sm: Hosts Kyle Peterson, Kim Strassel and Allysia Finley discuss House Republican leadership after the midterm losses. Speaker Mike Johnson said he will not seek the minority leader job, citing prayer and reflection and noting that Nancy Pelosi was the only modern speaker to stay on. Kim praises him for stepping aside and for leading a hard period, including passing the One Big Beautiful Bill. She says the race between Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan is close. Scalise argues he is tested and has been through a minority before, but many of his allies just lost their seats. Jordan argues the party needs a fresh approach, and he has the Freedom Caucus endorsement and must win over moderates.

The discussion turns to California, where a one time wealth tax initiative failed by about four percentage points even as Democrats won every statewide office and expanded their supermajorities. Allysia says the backers, including a health care workers union, have not conceded and may try again in 2028 or push a big income tax increase through the legislature. At least seven billionaires holding about 580 billion dollars have already left. She warns that when AI driven capital gains fade, deficits will follow and the state may target businesses, for example by lifting the property tax cap. Asked whether California's ballot is too easy to get onto, she says the real issue is Democratic control of the legislature and courts, pointing to a 2024 business backed measure that was kicked off the ballot.

The panel discusses the claim that billionaires buy elections, noting that Elon Musk reportedly spent about 220 million dollars in Texas and Republicans still lost. Kim says Republicans outspent Democrats in Texas, Ohio, Maine and Michigan, yet lost because money is only one factor and the party lacked a forward agenda. She calls Ken Paxton a scandal prone candidate and says Susan Collins paid for her ties to Donald Trump. Kyle notes record midterm spending of about 12 billion dollars is comparable to what Americans spend yearly on vitamins or cookies. Allysia then introduces the Supreme Court case Department of Labor versus Sun Valley Orchards, in which a New Jersey farm was fined about 550,000 dollars over worker meal arrangements.

Allysia explains that the orchard, which went out of business in 2021, was penalized through the Labor Department's administrative process and now invokes the Seventh Amendment and the 2024 Jarkesy decision on jury trials. The government argues the case falls under an immigration related public rights exception. The hosts play an exchange in which Justice Samuel Alito asks how far that exception extends, and the orchard's lawyer says it covers granting or revoking a benefit but not monetary liability. Kim argues the claim is a breach of private contract, a traditional common law matter, and cites the Third Circuit saying the case falls outside the heartland of non Article Three adjudication. She says a ruling for the orchard would strengthen Jarkesy and the separation of powers.
